questions.statement: I ___ in Paris twice, and both trips were wonderful.
questions.context: The experience happened at an unspecified time before now.

options.feedback: Correct! Life experience with no stated past time is expressed with the present perfect.
The past simple would need a finished past time, such as in 2019, to justify this use.
A present continuous would describe a current or imminent trip, not two completed journeys.
The past perfect needs a past reference point before the journeys, and there is none.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect with have been covers experience at any time up to now when the time is irrelevant. Twice tells us the number, not the date.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We ___ the treaty in 1998, and it is still in force.
questions.context: A past action with an explicit finished time.

options.feedback: Correct! A finished past time such as in 1998 requires the past simple.
The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time, because then the action would no longer relate to now.
A future form contradicts a date that has already passed.
A present continuous would place the signing in the present, which the year makes impossible.

questions.explanation:
A precise finished past time locks the action into the past. The still in force clause reports the present result, but the signing itself is simply past.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He ___ in this city for twelve years.
questions.context: The period began in the past and is still open now.

options.feedback: Correct! For with a duration that reaches the present calls for the present perfect.
The past simple would suggest the living ended, and it does not work with the for phrase used in this open sense.
The present continuous works with for only in the sense of a temporary or non-permanent arrangement.
The past perfect would place the twelve years before another past point, and there is none in the sentence.

questions.explanation:
For plus a period of time is a signature of the present perfect, because the period reaches up to now. For twelve years in this city means she still lives there.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ you ever ___ in a helicopter?
questions.context: A result is important in the present, so no past time is given.

options.feedback: Correct! Ever belongs to the present perfect and is used with the participle after have.
Did with ever is not the standard form, and did asks about a definite past moment.
The present perfect needs the past participle flown, not the -ing form flying.
Do builds the present simple and cannot be combined with ever in this way.

questions.explanation:
Ever is a present perfect marker. The structure is have plus ever plus past participle, with the subject and the auxiliary in the right order in the question.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She ___ never ___ spicy food in her life.
questions.context: A negative statement covering the whole period up to now.

options.feedback: Correct! In her life covers all time up to now, so the present perfect negative is correct.
Did refers to a definite past moment, while in her life is deliberately open ended.
After have the verb must be a past participle, and ate is the past simple form.
A present continuous would describe an action happening now, not the whole life up to now.

questions.explanation:
Expressions such as in her life, so far and up to now all point to the present perfect, in both the affirmative and the negative. The participle form is what follows has.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He ___ his homework an hour ago, so he is free now.
questions.context: The action is finished and the exact time is stated.

options.feedback: Correct! An hour ago is a finished past time, so the past simple is used.
The present perfect cannot stand with an hour ago, because that time cuts the action off from the present.
The present simple would make the finishing a habit, but the sentence reports one finished action.
The present perfect continuous would need an open period still going on.

questions.explanation:
The rule is about the time expression, not about the result. A finished past time such as an hour ago, yesterday or in 2010 always takes the past simple.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It ___ since six this morning, and it has not stopped once.
questions.context: The activity started in the past and is still running.

options.feedback: Correct! Since six this morning with an activity still running takes the present perfect continuous.
The past simple would present the rain as over, while has not stopped once shows it continues.
The present continuous would lose the link with the starting time given by since.
The past perfect continuous would need a past reference point, and this morning is still today.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect continuous emphasises duration from a past start up to now. Since plus a clock time is one of its clearest markers, and the continuing result confirms it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: They ___ married for eight years before they moved abroad.
questions.context: A finished period measured from a point in the past.

options.feedback: Correct! The past perfect continuous measures a period completed before another past event, the move.
The present perfect continuous cannot look back from a past event such as the move.
A present continuous would place the marriage in the present, which the move contradicts.
The future perfect projects forward from a future point, and the move is in the past.

questions.explanation:
Before they moved abroad is a past reference point. Measuring a duration that ended at that point requires had plus been plus the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ you ___ the results yet?
questions.context: A recent action whose present result is the point of the sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! Yet belongs to the present perfect and asks about a result that has not arrived.
Did with yet is not used, because yet places the question in the present period.
The present perfect needs the participle received, not the -ing form.
A future form would ask about an expectation, not about whether the result is already in.

questions.explanation:
Yet is another present perfect marker, used for things expected but not yet received. The question is about the present state of the result.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ three emails since I sat down this morning.
questions.context: A non-continuous verb completed within an open period.

options.feedback: Correct! A countable verb completed in a period that reaches now takes the present perfect.
The past simple would need a finished past time, but since I sat down keeps the period open.
A present continuous would suggest the sending is going on right now rather than completed three times.
The past perfect would place the emails before another past point, which the sentence does not have.

questions.explanation:
With verbs that do not continue, the present perfect counts completed actions inside an open period. Continuous verbs take the continuous form and count events the same way.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The museum ___ from its collection, but the catalogue still lists the painting.
questions.context: The information is no longer available.

options.feedback: Correct! The catalogue still lists it, so the removal is relevant in the present.
The past simple would leave the present relevance unstated, and the contradiction with the catalogue needs the link to now.
A present continuous would suggest the removal is still under way, which the catalogue does not support.
The past perfect would need a past point to look back from, and there is none.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect is used when a past action explains the present. The still lists clause is the present state that makes the present perfect necessary.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I didn't go to the concert, ___ because I had no money then.
questions.context: A negative statement about a period in the past that has closed.

options.feedback: Correct! Because introduces the reason for a negative past statement.
Although would contrast two facts without giving the reason, so the causal link is lost.
So gives a result, and the sentence is explaining a cause rather than a consequence.
Unless introduces a condition, and no condition is being proposed here.

questions.explanation:
A negative past statement often takes because to explain the cause. The reason for not going is given directly, and a contrast would need although or however.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: They ___ in the same town all their lives, and they are not planning to leave.
questions.context: The form of the present perfect with an irregular verb.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Live' takes lived in the past participle, so the correct form is have lived.
The spelling is wrong: the past participle of live is lived, with no extra i.
After have the verb must be a past participle, and the base form live does not work here.
A present continuous with all their lives is possible for a temporary arrangement, but it loses the open duration.

questions.explanation:
Regular verbs add -ed to the participle, and live simply doubles the final e. All their lives is the open period that points to the present perfect.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Have you ___ the invitation from the mayor yet?
questions.context: The sentence needs the participle, not the past simple.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Receive' is a regular verb and its past participle is received.
That is not a word in English; the participle of receive is received.
The -ing form belongs to continuous tenses, not to the present perfect.
Receives is the third person singular present form and cannot follow have.

questions.explanation:
Regular verbs form the participle with -ed, and the spelling of receive keeps the e. What matters is that the word after have is a participle, not a base form.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I ___ never ___ such a long exam in my life.
questions.context: The state began in the past and still holds.

options.feedback: Correct! Never and in my life both point to the present perfect, and sit has the irregular participle sat.
Did is for a definite past moment, while in my life covers all of the past up to now.
Sitted is not the participle; the correct irregular participle of sit is sat.
A present continuous would describe a current action and cannot cover the whole life.

questions.explanation:
Never and in my life are present perfect markers, and the participle of sit is sat. Both halves of the sentence work together to close the period at now.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: They ___ in La Paz since 2010, and they still go there every year.
questions.context: A state that is still true, expressed with a stative verb.

options.feedback: Correct! Since 2010 with a state that continues is expressed with the present perfect.
The past simple would suggest they no longer live there, and the since phrase rules that out.
A present continuous would suggest the arrangement is temporary or not permanent.
The past perfect would need a past point to look back from, and since 2010 is not that.

questions.explanation:
Since plus a year is a present perfect marker, and the second clause confirms that the state continues. The two clauses together rule out every past tense.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The committee ___ the budget on 5 March and announced it the same evening.
questions.context: The action was performed on a date and there is no present relevance.

options.feedback: Correct! The date closes the action in the past, so the past simple is correct.
The present perfect cannot be used with a finished past date such as 5 March.
The present simple would place the approval in the present, which the date denies.
A past continuous would suggest the approval was still in progress, which it was not.

questions.explanation:
A precise date is a finished past time. The present perfect is reserved for actions whose present relevance is being reported, and none is reported here.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ you ___ anything to eat since breakfast?
questions.context: A short unfinished period, expressed with a countable verb.

options.feedback: Correct! Since breakfast starts an open period, and the participle of have is had.
Did is not used with since, because since keeps the period reaching the present.
After have the verb must be a participle, and having is the -ing form.
A present continuous question would ask about the moment of speaking, not the period since breakfast.

questions.explanation:
Since plus a meal or a moment of the day opens a period that is still open at the moment of speaking. The countable verb take therefore appears in the present perfect with had.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The delegation ___ at the airport; the officials are waiting outside.
questions.context: The person has arrived and the arrival matters now.

options.feedback: Correct! The waiting officials show the arrival is complete and relevant now.
The past simple would leave the present moment open, and the officials waiting outside closes it.
A present continuous would suggest the plane is still on its way, not that the arrival is complete.
A future form contradicts the officials already waiting for the delegation.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect reports a completed arrival whose consequence is happening now. The second clause is the present evidence that the tense must reach up to now.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She ___ the report, ___ she has read every article twice.
questions.context: A negative sentence contrasting two activities in the same period.

options.feedback: Correct! But contrasts the unfinished report with the completed reading, both inside the present period.
Did places the actions in a finished past moment, and so would give a result rather than a contrast.
Because gives a reason, and the second clause is not the reason why the report is unfinished.
A past continuous would place the first action in a past scene that the present perfect reading contradicts.

questions.explanation: Both activities belong to the present period, so both need the present perfect, and but marks the contrast. Choosing the connector changes the meaning of the whole sentence.
questions.subject: ingles
